title: Curry Cruiser Revised
tagline: A structured Thai curry ordering flow that keeps customization clear for customers and prep details readable for staff.
overview: Curry Cruiser Revised explores a mobile-first ordering experience for a Thai curry food truck where customers customize orders through predefined choices instead of free-text notes.

The work balances two user needs: customers need to order quickly and confidently under food truck time pressure, while staff need complete, supported, consistently formatted tickets during rush service.

The final direction is Curry Builder With Staff-Ready Review, a lightweight responsive flow with guided curry choices, review-before-submit, optional QR/direct/staff entry, confirmation, and compact staff ticket output.
problem: Customers may hesitate or submit incomplete curry orders when menu choices, spice levels, pickup details, or QR access feel unclear; staff may lose time interpreting ambiguous, unsupported, or incomplete order details.
solution: Model curry ordering as required, clearly grouped choices with short food-language guidance, structured dietary and pickup details, a human-readable review step, visible fallback paths, and staff-readable ticket sequencing.
role: UX research synthesis, product definition, ideation, wireframe requirements, and case study assembly
timeline: Stage 01 through Stage 06 revised case study run
highlights: Separated QR access from the core value proposition so scanning stays optional.
Turned the no-free-text constraint into required modifier-style groups.
Linked first-time menu uncertainty to short curry and spice explanations.
Made staff ticket readability a primary user need.
Kept payment, accounts, loyalty, delivery, and free-text requests out of first scope.

process.title: Research
process.summary: Desk research validated the broad plausibility of mobile off-premises ordering, food truck speed pressure, structured modifiers, QR ordering feasibility, and accessible form patterns while flagging Curry Cruiser-specific gaps.
insights: Mobile ordering is directionally valid for a food truck context, but the flow must stay fast and lightweight.
Structured restaurant modifiers support predefined customization better than blank notes.
QR access is feasible, but QR-only ordering creates adoption and accessibility risk.

process.title: Empathize
process.summary: Synthetic participant artifacts represented time-pressed customers, first-time curry customers, QR-cautious customers, and rush-period staff because real interviews were unavailable.
insights: Speed only helps if customers can still review and trust the order.
Unfamiliar curry and spice labels need short guidance.
Staff need valid, complete orders they can scan quickly.

process.title: Define
process.summary: The definition phase narrowed the challenge to balancing customer confidence, speed, menu guidance, optional access, and staff-readable structure without overclaiming unvalidated details.
insights: The problem is not simply making ordering digital.
Staff clarity is a user need, not a back-office afterthought.
Payment, pickup process, menu structure, and allergy policy remain validation targets.

process.title: Ideate
process.summary: Ideation combined a guided builder, staff prep sequence, confidence review, QR fallback entry, allergy guardrails, and pickup ticket into one focused ordering direction.
insights: The strongest concept is a mobile-first structured builder with clear review and confirmation.
Feature scope should exclude unvalidated payment, accounts, loyalty, delivery, order history, and free-text requests.
Fallback, disabled, loading, error, and success states are part of the first prototype requirements.

process.title: Prototype Direction
process.summary: The wireframe requirements define an entry screen, curry selection, protein/base selection, spice/add-ons, dietary and pickup details, order review, and confirmation/pickup ticket.
insights: Review and confirmation should be explicit screens, not implied states.
Submitted order data should follow a compact prep-readable sequence.
Severe allergies and failed submission states should route customers to staff rather than accepting risky free text.

userThreads.sourceInsight: Time-pressed customers may be digitally comfortable but still need visible required choices, quick review, and unmistakable confirmation before the flow feels faster than talking to staff.
sourceArtifacts: Journey Map: Riley, The Time-Pressed Regular

persona.name: Riley
persona.summary: A lunch customer ordering near the truck between commitments who wants a fast, accurate curry order and a clear pickup cue.

userThreads.userStory: As a time-pressed food truck customer, I want to customize my usual curry quickly and review it before submission, so that I can skip avoidable line friction without worrying about mistakes.

journeySummary.scenario: Riley opens the ordering link near the truck, chooses required curry details, reviews the order, submits, and waits for pickup.
journeySummary.keyPainPoint: Fast ordering breaks down when required choices, final review, or pickup confirmation are unclear.
journeySummary.opportunity: Use concise required sections, a plain review screen, and a confirmation tied to pickup.

userThreads.designImpact: The flow avoids account-heavy friction, keeps required selections visible, and includes review plus confirmation as speed-supporting features.

userThreads.sourceInsight: First-time customers can be interested in Thai curry but hesitate when curry names, spice levels, or included ingredients are not explained.
sourceArtifacts: Journey Map: Maya, The Curious First-Timer

persona.name: Maya
persona.summary: A first-time event customer who wants to try Curry Cruiser without guessing what curry type or spice level will match her taste.

userThreads.userStory: As a first-time Curry Cruiser customer, I want short guidance on curry types and spice levels, so that I can choose confidently without asking staff to explain the whole menu.

journeySummary.scenario: Maya browses curry options, compares taste and spice cues, customizes the bowl, reviews the plain-language order, and picks it up.
journeySummary.keyPainPoint: Option names alone do not give enough confidence for unfamiliar curry and spice decisions.
journeySummary.opportunity: Pair predefined options with short taste descriptions, spice scale language, and included/default notes.

userThreads.designImpact: The wireframes use short option descriptions, recommended markers only when validated, and human-readable review copy instead of POS shorthand.

userThreads.sourceInsight: Staff working during rush service need complete, supported, consistently ordered tickets because free-text notes and missing choices slow preparation.
sourceArtifacts: Journey Map: Jordan, The Peak-Service Expediter

persona.name: Jordan
persona.summary: A Curry Cruiser staff member who prepares orders and manages handoff in a noisy, time-sensitive food truck environment.

userThreads.userStory: As a Curry Cruiser staff member, I want every submitted order to use complete and supported choices, so that I can prepare it accurately without stopping service to clarify details.

journeySummary.scenario: Jordan receives a ticket, scans modifiers, prepares the curry, calls the pickup identifier, and resolves exceptions during rush service.
journeySummary.keyPainPoint: Ambiguous notes, invalid choices, and inconsistent ticket order interrupt prep flow.
journeySummary.opportunity: Enforce required supported choices and format the submitted order in prep-readable sequence.

userThreads.designImpact: Customer-facing flexibility is bounded by operational feasibility, and the confirmation includes a compact staff-readable ticket sequence.

keyDecisions.decision: Use required grouped choices instead of free-text customization.
keyDecisions.why: Stage 01 set no-free-text ordering as a constraint, and Stage 02 found that restaurant modifier systems support predefined options, limits, ordering, and ticket display.
keyDecisions.impact: Customers cannot submit missing core prep details, and staff receive more consistent orders.

keyDecisions.decision: Make curry and spice guidance part of the selection UI.
keyDecisions.why: Maya's synthetic evidence showed that unfamiliar curry names and subjective spice labels can create hesitation.
keyDecisions.impact: First-time customers get enough context to choose without asking staff to explain the full menu.

keyDecisions.decision: Keep review-before-submit in the core flow.
keyDecisions.why: Riley and cautious users need confidence that the order is correct before sending it, and accessible form guidance supports clear final actions near the end of the task.
keyDecisions.impact: Customers can catch mistakes before submission, reducing post-submit corrections.

keyDecisions.decision: Offer QR, direct URL, and staff-assisted entry.
keyDecisions.why: QR ordering is feasible, but Stage 02 identified device, connectivity, accessibility, and preference risks.
keyDecisions.impact: The flow can serve QR-comfortable customers without excluding customers who cannot or do not want to scan.

keyDecisions.decision: Route severe allergies and complex exceptions to staff.
keyDecisions.why: The project avoids free text, and allergy handling is operationally and legally unvalidated.
keyDecisions.impact: The prototype does not pretend complex safety needs can be safely resolved through predefined checkboxes alone.

keyDecisions.decision: Exclude payment, accounts, loyalty, delivery, order history, and kitchen dashboard from first scope.
keyDecisions.why: Payment and pickup workflow are unknown, and the evidence points to a lightweight ordering task rather than a full restaurant platform.
keyDecisions.impact: The first prototype stays focused on order completion, customer confidence, and staff readability.

validation: Interview real Curry Cruiser customers and staff to replace synthetic participant evidence.
Validate the actual menu categories, supported combinations, dietary flags, sold-out behavior, payment model, and pickup identifiers.
Run a first-time menu comprehension test where users explain their selected curry and spice level after completing the flow.
Run a staff ticket scan test to see whether required prep details can be identified in five seconds or less.
Test QR-comfortable and QR-cautious users on entry, fallback discovery, review, submission, and confirmation.
outcome: The revised case study establishes a credible prototype direction with medium support for the broad mobile, structured-ordering, and food truck context, but low direct confidence in Curry Cruiser-specific behavior because all participant artifacts are synthetic and the real menu, workflow, payment, pickup, and allergy policies remain unvalidated.
nextSteps: Confirm Curry Cruiser's real menu options and operationally valid modifier groups.
Run the Stage 02 customer and staff interview plan.
Prototype the mobile flow in low fidelity and test order completion.
Validate the staff-readable ticket format during rush-like review.
Decide whether payment belongs in a later scope.
